The Lineated barbet (Psilopogon lineatus) hatches from its incubated egg after a defined developmental period. The eggs, which are incubated by both parents, typically require 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days] to hatch when maintained at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This incubation duration is consistent with values reported for other medium-sized Asian barbets. Upon emergence, the altricial nestling possesses a relatively low initial wet weight of 10.5 grams [Ww0 = 10.5 grams], with field observations indicating a range of 10.2 to 11.8 grams for this mass at hatching. This modest body mass at the start of life underscores the substantial parental investment required during the subsequent nestling period, as the chick is entirely dependent on its parents for both thermoregulation and provisioning of fruit and insects.

As the chick develops within the nest cavity, it undergoes a period of rapid mass gain before it is ready to fledge. Under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of this species, approximately 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], the nestling achieves its first flight and departs the nest at 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching]. This fledging age is based on the hatching event and marks the transition to a fledgling capable of short flights, though it remains dependent on its parents for food for several weeks thereafter. The energetic costs incurred during this nestling phase are significant, with basal metabolic rate measurements from respirometry trials on resting individuals yielding a maximum oxygen consumption of 131.65 milliliters per hour [JOi = 131.65 milliliters per hour] recorded at the same body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].

The onset of reproductive capability in this species follows a distinct developmental schedule. Gonadal maturation and the attainment of sexual maturity occur at 75 days since birth [tp = 75 days since birth], a value documented under field conditions at the species' typical active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. However, the initiation of actual breeding activity, or the age at first brood, is deferred substantially beyond puberty. The first successful reproductive event is typically recorded at 620.5 days after hatching [tR = 620.5 days after hatching]; this delay likely reflects the time required for a young bird to establish a territory, secure a mate, and acquire the necessary foraging experience to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].

The reproductive output of a breeding pair is modest in terms of annual fecundity. Females produce clutches ranging from 2 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 4 eggs per clutch], with only a single clutch attempted each year [F_R_i = single clutch attempted each year] under the thermal regime of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This low annual reproductive rate is characteristic of many tropical cavity-nesting species and is thought to be balanced by relatively high adult survival. The ultimate body mass attained by adults shows a clear sexual size dimorphism, with females reaching a maximum adult body mass of 156 grams [Wwi = 156 grams], while males are somewhat smaller, with a recorded ultimate wet weight of 146 grams [Wwi = 146 grams]. This difference in mass may relate to the energetic costs of egg production in females.

The overall lifespan of this species reflects its position on the slow end of the life-history continuum. Maximum recorded longevity for the Lineated barbet in the wild is 5,110 days [am = 5,110 days], a lifespan estimated from banding returns and observed at the typical active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This extended lifespan, combined with a low annual fecundity and delayed first reproduction, positions the species firmly within a slow life-history strategy typical of many tropical forest birds. Comparative data from related species within the Megalaimidae suggest that such longevity is not unusual for the group, which is characterized by stable, resource-rich environments. The trade-offs between high adult survival and low reproductive output are reinforced by the substantial somatic investment required to achieve the adult body masses of 146 and 156 grams.
